This exercise cleaned a customer data set across four columns: customer_name, order_id, order_date, and email. Rather than treating every missing value the same way, I worked through each column individually and documented the reasoning behind each decision, using both base R and tidyverse approaches.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
df_fmt1 <- data.frame(
  customer_name = c("Alice", "alex ", "  BOB", "nathan", "Charlie", " blake","Mark","David","James","Tom","Bill","Joe" ),
  order_id = c("A1","A2","A3","A4 ","A5 ","A6","A7","A9","A10 ","A11","A12 ","A13" ),
  order_date = c("2026-01-05", "01/06/2026", "2026/01/07",
                 "2026-01-08", "06-01-2026", "2026-01-10","2026-01-09", "01/12/2026", "2026/01/17",
                 "2026-01-08", "06-01-2026", "2026-01-10"),
  email = c("a@example.com", "a2@example.com", "b@example.com","k@example.com","x@example.com","k2@example.com","y4example.com","g1@example.com","pp@example.com",
            "b2@example.com", "c@example.com", "c2@example.com"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

library(lubridate)
library (tidyverse)
library(validate)

```

```{r}
#perview the raw, uncleaned data
df_fmt1
```

```{r}
#data inspection
dim(df_fmt1)
names(df_fmt1)
str(df_fmt1)
head(df_fmt1)
summary(df_fmt1)

```

## **Base R Version**

### Cleaning: "customer_name" — Case and Spacing Inconsistency

```{r}
unique((df_fmt1$customer_name)) #display unique value of column
unique(trimws(df_fmt1$customer_name)) #display inconsistencies with values
df_fmt1$customer_name <- trimws(df_fmt1$customer_name) #removes white spaces
df_fmt1$customer_name <- str_replace_all(df_fmt1$customer_name,"\\s*-\\s*", "-") #removes extra spacing
df_fmt1$customer_name <- str_to_title(df_fmt1$customer_name) #coverts text to proper casing
#verify that it worked
unique(df_fmt1$customer_name)
#run full data frame
df_fmt1
```

### Cleaning: "order_id" — Spacing Inconsistency

```{r}
unique(trimws(df_fmt1$order_id)) # displays inconsistencies with spacing
df_fmt1$order_id <- trimws(df_fmt1$order_id) # removes white spaces
df_fmt1$order_id <- str_replace_all(df_fmt1$order_id,"\\s*-\\s*", "-") #removes extra spacing- makes it uniform
#verify that it worked
unique(df_fmt1$order_id)
#run full data frame
df_fmt1

```

### Cleaning: "order_date — Covert Using Parsing

```{r}
unique(df_fmt1$order_date)# display the unique value of column
df_fmt1$order_date <- parse_date_time(df_fmt1$order_date,
                                      orders = c("ymd","mdy","dmy") #gives a proper date
                                      
)

df_fmt1$order_date <- as.Date(df_fmt1$order_date) #Converts to Date class
#verify that it worked
df_fmt1$order_date
#Create a formatted display version
df_fmt1$order_date_formatted <-format(df_fmt1$order_date,"%m-%d-%Y")
#run full data frame
df_fmt1
```

I parsed the date column using multiple possible formats so that values would be recognized correctly as dates. After converting the text into proper "Date" object, I verified the result and formatted the output for display using format(). This allowed me to keep the dates usable for analysis while also showing them in the m/d/Y style when needed.

### Cleaning: "email — Covert Invalid email to Valid email Format

```{r}
unique(df_fmt1$email) #display the unique values
df_fmt1[!grepl("@", df_fmt1$email), ] # to view rows that are missing @ sign
df_fmt1$email[df_fmt1$email == "y4example.com"] <- "y4@example.com" # to add the @ sign 
#verify that it worked
df_fmt1$email
#run full data frame
df_fmt1

```

Initially, I ran df_fmt1\$email \[df_fmt1\$email == "y4example.com\@"\] \<- "y4\@example.com" and saw no change int he data frame because R could not find the exact match for"y4example.com\@". After reviewing the data, I identified the correct value in the data frame and replace it.

## **What this showed me:**

I had to covert standardized data text into actual data objects after parsing multiple formats, then format them with format(df\$variable, "%d-%m\_%Y") for analysis and display".

## Tidyverse Version

To compare approaches, I repeated the same exercise using tidyverse syntax instead of base R.

### Cleaning: "customer_name" — Case and Spacing Inconsistency

```{r}
unique(df_fmt1$customer_name) # viewing the unique values
df_fmt1 <- df_fmt1 %>%
  mutate(customer_name = customer_name %>%
           str_trim() %>%
           str_to_title())
#verify that it worked
df_fmt1
```

### Cleaning: "order_id" — Spacing Inconsistency

```{r}
unique(df_fmt1$order_id) # view the unique values
df_fmt1 <- df_fmt1 %>%
  mutate(order_id = order_id %>%
           str_trim() %>%
           str_squish())
#verify that it worked
df_fmt1
```

### Cleaning: "order_date — Covert Using Parsing

```{r}
unique(df_fmt1$order_date) #view the unique values
df_fmt1 <- df_fmt1 %>%
  mutate(order_date = order_date %>%
           parse_date_time(order = c("ymd","mdy","dmy")))
#verify that it worked
df_fmt1$order_date
#Create a formatted display version
df_fmt1$order_date_formatted <-format(df_fmt1$order_date,"%m-%d-%Y")
#run full data frame
df_fmt1
```

### Cleaning: "email — Covert Invalid email to Valid email Format

```{r}
unique(df_fmt1$email)
df_fmt1 <- df_fmt1 %>%
  mutate(email = ifelse(email == "y4example.com", "y4@example.com", email)) 
#verify that it worked
df_fmt1

```

## **What this showed me:**

While cleaning data, I learned that different formats and methods can be used to achieve the needed data manipulation for interpretation. Through this process, I also learned that Tidyverse provides a shorter and easier way to work, especially when the pipe operators.
